catalog_quote: Kibushi, mainly used orally, is understudied despite its apparent rich and complex variation. It is linguistically close to the Sakalava Malagasy dialect from the northwest of Madagascar [2]. There are two dialects with limited intercomprehensability: Kisakalava, used in a dozen villages with some twenty thousand speakers, and Kiantalautsi, spoken mostly in two villages, Ouangani and Poroani, by a few thousand speakers [1]. ... Second, general observations of Kibushi suggest that there may be differences in word stress across villages and dialects. ... Stress in both Kibushi dialects is penultimate, just as in the Malagasy language (Merina dialect). But it can also fall on the antepenultimate syllable with words that end in [ka], [͡tra] and [na] [7]. ... Figure 3 shows the duration of stressed and unstressed syllables in Kibushi. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: confirmed verbatim at the stated pages in the held HAL PDF; locator correct. (2) Source: a 2023 ICPhS pilot instrumental study; the position rule ('penultimate; can also be antepenultimate with final [ka]/[tra]/[na]') is an introductory assertion whose conditional clause cites a Merina intonation paper (Aziz & Paul 2019), so for stress POSITION the evidence is effectively second-hand pan-Malagasy lore applied to Kibushi, backed only by the authors' penult-stressed Swadesh items. Identity is only partly on-glottocode: Kisakalava = kibu1236 (anta1255) but Kiantalautsi = kian1236 under Glottolog's separate language bush1250 [buc]; mainland Antankarana [main1284] is undescribed in anything held. The record's own notes already flag most of this (the C adjudication text treats both Kibushi dialects as anta1255, which Glottolog 5.x does not). (3) Better sources exist but are offline:

sources.note: Glottolog's MED for anta1255 and the only full grammar with a phonology part for the Northern Sakalava/Antankarana mainland area; our coding rests on one background sentence in a 4-page Mayotte pilot study whose antepenult clause is imported from a Merina paper. Would settle whether the weak-final-syllable set is [ka]/[tra]/[na] as in Merina or has northern reflexes, and whether the antepenult class is lexical.
